Official Scope + Resources

1. Explain the importance and benefits of patient-centered communication (PCC).
2. Define the three elements of PCC.
3. Demonstrate basic PCC skills including agenda negotiation, empathy, OARS, and ask-tell-ask / ask-respond-tell.
4. Identify advanced PCC including motivational interviewing and brief action planning.

Preview handout page 3. The four 2025 lecture objectives match the 2026 Week 9 HPC objectives in substance: why PCC matters, the three elements, basic communication skills, and advanced PCC.
Best mental map: Start by building rapport and setting an agenda → Explore the patient’s perspective and context → Respond with empathy → Share information with ATA/ART and teach-back → Plan together using MI or brief action planning when behavior change is the goal.

Why Patient-Centered Communication?

The relationship matters

The handout anchors PCC in compassion, dignity, and respect. It also states that the patient-provider relationship is the strongest predictive factor of psychotherapy outcomes, with goal consensus second.

Listening does not necessarily take longer

The poll asks how long patients speak before interruption; the next slide gives an average of 11 seconds. It also notes that visits where physicians respond to emotional clues are, on average, 3 minutes shorter.

Preview handout page 6. The slide connects ethics, listening behavior, emotional responsiveness, relationship quality, and shared goals.
Patient vs provider: the handout reports only moderate agreement between self-rated and provider-rated health (r = 0.45), with physicians more influenced by physical factors and patients more influenced by psychosocial factors. That mismatch is exactly why eliciting the patient’s perspective is not optional.

The “difficult” patient is relational, not just patient-based

The handout estimates ~15% of patients are viewed as “difficult,” then deliberately splits contributors across patient factors, physician factors, and health-system factors. The framing discourages reflexively locating the whole problem in the patient.

The Three Elements of PCC

1 · Elicit perspective

Learn how the patient understands the illness, what they fear, what they expect, and what matters most to them.

2 · Understand psychosocial context

Place the illness inside the patient’s life rather than treating the biomedical problem as if it exists by itself.

3 · Reach shared goals

Develop treatment goals that align with the patient’s values rather than simply delivering a plan to the patient.

Preview handout page 10. The handout’s PCC model: perspective + psychosocial context + shared goals aligned with patient values.

Starting the Visit

Build rapport

Introductions and small talk establish the relationship before the agenda begins.

Cast the net wide

Lead with a visit-focused open question such as “What brings you in today?”

Exhaust the list

Use “What else?” before narrowing the agenda so hidden concerns do not appear at the end.

Negotiate the agenda

Ask which concern is most important and transparently add clinician priorities: “I would also like to discuss…”

Preview handout page 11. Rapport → broad opening → “what else?” → negotiated agenda.
Practical sequence: “What brings you in today?” → “What else?” → “Anything else?” → “Which of these is most important to make sure we address today?” → “I would also like to discuss…”

Exploring the Visit: OARS + Patient Perspective

Facilitate, do not interrogate

Verbal facilitators include “Go on,” “Mm-hmm,” and “Ahh.” Nonverbal facilitators include eye contact, head nodding, and leaning forward.

OARS

Open questions · Affirmations · Reflective listening · Summarizing.

Preview handout page 12. OARS sits beside five perspective domains: feelings, ideas, concerns, impact, and expectations.
Feelings
“How do you feel about that?”
Ideas
“What do you think is the cause?”
Concerns
“What do you fear happening?”
Impact
“What difficulties does this create?”
Expectations
“What do you need today?”
Exam-level takeaway
The point is not just asking more questions; it is discovering the patient’s explanatory model, stakes, and desired outcome.
Ozzy found the hidden concern: “What else?” before you close the agenda. 🐾

Empathy: Understand + Communicate Understanding

Four qualities

1. See the world as others do
2. Be nonjudgmental
3. Understand others’ emotions
4. Communicate that understanding

What empathy sounds like

The handout includes partnership, apology, respect, legitimization, support, naming, understanding, and exploration statements.

Preview handout page 14. Examples include “Let’s work together,” “It seems like you are feeling…,” “I see why that’s upsetting,” and “Tell me more about…”
SkillHandout examplePurpose
Partnership“Let’s work together.”Signals collaboration
Naming“It seems like you are feeling…”Makes emotion discussable
Legitimization“Most people would feel the same.”Validates the response without judging it
Understanding“I see why that’s upsetting.”Communicates the clinician’s understanding
Exploring“Tell me more about…”Invites depth instead of closing the topic

Ending the Visit: Orient, Summarize, Check Understanding

Orient to the end

Give the patient a time cue such as “We have a few minutes left…” rather than abruptly ending the visit.

Summarize

Use language such as “Here’s what I’ve heard…” or “If I’m understanding correctly…”

Preview handout page 15. The handout places Ask-Tell-Ask and Ask-Respond-Tell loops alongside teach-back and notes they can be used throughout the encounter, not just at the end.
ATA / ART principle: do not simply dump information. First learn what the patient knows or wants to know, share information responsively, then check the new understanding.

Advanced PCC: Motivational Interviewing + Brief Action Planning

Motivational interviewing

The handout describes MI as a process, style, and spirit of communication with four parts: engaging → focusing → evoking → planning. It also highlights developing discrepancy and “rolling with resistance.”

Brief Action Planning

The slide begins by asking whether the patient would like to do something for their health, then moves through an optional behavioral menu, a SMART action plan, commitment, confidence scaling, barrier-solving if confidence is below 7, and a follow-up check.

Preview handout page 16. MI and Brief Action Planning are the advanced PCC tools emphasized in the handout.
Do not confuse basic PCC with advanced PCC. Agenda negotiation, empathy, OARS, and ATA/ART are basic encounter skills in this lecture; MI and Brief Action Planning are the advanced behavior-change tools.
